On Friday, OpenAI Group PBC, its hardware unit io Products and former Apple employees Chang Liu and Tang Yew Tan filed counterclaims against Apple in federal court in San Jose, answering the trade-secret suit Apple brought in July. The 81-page counterclaim filing in Apple v. OpenAI (case 5:26-cv-07078, document 217) denies Apple’s main allegations and turns several of them around. According to Reuters’ report on OpenAI’s countersuit, OpenAI says Apple obtained confidential information by rehiring a former employee who spent six months at OpenAI and had access to details of a new device and OpenAI’s roadmap for future hardware. The filing calls that person “Employee X” and says his last day at OpenAI was June 2, 2026. The BBC’s account of the counterclaims says OpenAI accuses him of sending “dozens of OpenAI documents” to his personal phone numbers and then presenting OpenAI’s plans to senior Apple staff “at Apple’s request.” The supplier allegations may matter more commercially. The filing says Apple’s supply-management staff demanded that shared vendors identify workers assigned to OpenAI, that one manufacturer stopped doing OpenAI work it had previously handled, and that another moved OpenAI work to a nighttime shift of an anodizing process in a shared facility after Apple objected. Data Phoenix’s summary of the counterclaims notes OpenAI is seeking damages and narrowly tailored court orders, is challenging an Apple provision limiting recruiting of its staff for a year after departure, and that the court has set trial for July 19, 2027. OpenAI also says 400 employees have left Apple for OpenAI so far and argues Apple encourages staff to mix work files with personal iCloud accounts so it can later accuse departing employees of theft. According to Commercial Times, GUC has secured Tesla’s AI5 project alongside orders from Microsoft and Google, though tightening N3 capacity at TSMC could constrain the chip’s ramp-up. Electric Vehicle News, citing Tesla CEO Elon Musk, notes that Tesla will retain its existing AI4 self-driving hardware in vehicles, while prioritizing its next-generation AI5 chip for the Optimus humanoid robot. Tesla’s phased AI5 rollout aligns with GUC’s reported capacity priorities. According to Commercial Times, GUC is expected to prioritize its limited N3 capacity for major North American CSP projects, including Google’s Axion 2 and Axion 3 server processors and Microsoft’s in-house chips. Despite securing a substantially larger 3nm wafer allocation from TSMC for 2027, GUC still faces a capacity shortfall relative to demand from its major customers, the report adds. Supply chain sources cited by Commercial Times note that large-scale AI5 deployment in EVs may have to wait until 2028, when additional N3 capacity comes online and supply constraints ease. Reinforcing the importance of cloud orders to GUC, Economic Daily News notes that a U.S. CSP’s 3nm CPU ramp-up has been the primary driver of the company’s strong 2026 performance and is expected to sustain growth through 2027. The customer’s next-generation CPU, slated for tape-out between late 2026 and early 2027, could reportedly provide further momentum. Beyond its 3nm projects, GUC is also making inroads into 2nm ASICs. According to Investor.com, the company has finalized its HBM4E PHY and controller IP, which have already been adopted in a customer’s AI ASIC featuring TSMC’s advanced N2P process and CoWoS-L packaging. ---

The ADK complements the foundry's traditional process design kits (PDKs) and enables AI agents to use TSMC's process-specific expertise, knowledge of electronic design automation (EDA) tools, and customers' proprietary design methodologies to automate physical implementation and optimization of chips. Ultimately, the initiative aims to reduce development cycles, improve design productivity, and simplify adoption of TSMC's advanced process technologies. Add to that a greater number of metallization stack options and plenty of EDA tool settings, and the number of possible design configurations becomes massive. As a result, conventional design optimization methodologies approach their productivity limits, according to TSMC. At the same time, some of TSMC's customers want to reduce their chip development cycles from 18 months to 12 months, Sarkar said. items.excerpt: This week in AI rules: 21–27 November 2026 Our weekly roundup of AI rules this week: Australia passes a duty of care law covering AI chatbots, plus US state lawsuits, tracker changes and dates ahead. By AI Ethiquettes Desk, edited by Vijai G.· November 28, 2026· 3 min read AI rules this week kept coming back to children’s safety. Australia’s Senate passed a law that puts AI chatbots under the same duty of care as social media, while Oregon and Virginia sued OpenAI and the companies behind Grok under ordinary consumer law. The big story On 25 November Australia’s Senate approved the Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026, after Labor reached a deal with the Greens. The fault last unleashed a major earthquake in 1717, and geoscientists estimate a 75% probability of a rupture of magnitude 7 or greater occurring within the next 50 years. Yet predicting how violently the ground will shake or how far a rupture might tear has long been hindered by our inability to observe inside the fault zone at depth in fine enough detail. The findings are published in the journal Science Advances. Listening with sound in darkness By repurposing an existing commercial broadband fiber-optic cable into a massive, hypersensitive seismic antenna, the team captured the sharpest view ever achieved of the Alpine Fault's internal architecture. Working with Chorus, New Zealand's largest telecommunications company, they sent laser pulses down an unused, or dark, strand of optical fiber running 30 kilometers (19 miles) along the Haast Pass highway. As seismic waves pass through Earth, they microscopically stretch and compress the glass fiber. items.title: Runaway pulsar escapes the remnant of its own supernova
items.excerpt: Rohit Dokara and his team at the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy discovered a pulsar that has escaped the debris cloud from its own supernova explosion. The team made the discovery by analyzing combined radio observations from surveys conducted over the past two decades, adding to only about four known cases of such events. A pulsar is a magnetized, rapidly rotating neutron star that emits beams of radiation from its poles. These objects form when massive star cores collapse in supernova explosions, which create expanding shells of gas and dust called supernova remnants. During the initial explosion, pulsars often receive powerful kicks that propel them away from the shell's center. Dokara's team initially set out to investigate why astronomers estimate roughly 2,000 supernova remnants should exist in the Milky Way, yet only about 400 have been discovered. Using radio images and pulsar timing measurements, they calculated three factors for any pulsar-remnant pair: the pulsar's age based on how its spin slows, its angular separation from the shell center, and its distance from Earth. While combing through the data, Dokara found a previously unnoticed association. A new supernova remnant shell and a known pulsar, designated J1909+0749, lay well outside the shell, with the pulsar's tail pointing clearly toward the shell's center. The team estimated the pulsar's transverse velocity at over 1,400 kilometers per second, making it one of the fastest Milky Way pulsars. The discovery was made possible by MeerKAT, one of the latest generation of radio telescopes. Dokara noted that "the science potential for each such survey is enormous," and he expects similar observations could appear regularly in future large-scale surveys using newer facilities with improved sensitivity and resolution. The results are accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics and are available on the arXiv preprint server. This article summarizes reporting by Phys.org. ---

items.title: WHO urges action to close measles immunity gaps as South-East Asia countries account for 47% of global cases despite highest immunization coverage
items.excerpt: 28 November 2026 Despite having the highest measles vaccination coverage globally, the WHO South-East Asia Region accounted for 47% of estimated measles cases worldwide in 2025, highlighting persistent immunity gaps and the urgent need to accelerate efforts to interrupt transmission. An estimated 4.6 million measles cases and 16 800 deaths occurred in the Region in 2025. The Region achieved 96% coverage with the first dose of measles-containing vaccine (MCV1) and 93% with the second dose (MCV2), yet approximately 1.1 million infants missed their first dose. While measles cases in the Region declined by 59% and deaths by 90% since 2000, continued endemic transmission and multiple outbreaks in 2026 highlight the fragility of this progress. Vaccination has averted an estimated 12.3 million measles deaths in the Region since 2000. “High vaccination coverage at the regional or national level can create a false sense of security if children and communities remain unprotected. Measles is extremely contagious, and even small pockets of unvaccinated or under-vaccinated populations can sustain transmission and trigger outbreaks. Countries must ensure that every child receives both doses of the measles vaccine, wherever they live and whatever their circumstances,” said Dr Nilesh Buddha, Officer-in-Charge, WHO South-East Asia Region. items.title: Bangladesh Measles Outbreak 2026: Death Toll Climbs to 1,378 as Seven More Children Die in 24 Hours
items.excerpt: By Nafisa Syarif Published 28 November 2026, 2:10 PM +06 Bangladesh is battling a prolonged and deadly measles outbreak that shows little sign of abating. Health authorities confirmed seven more deaths linked to measles and measles-like symptoms in a single 24-hour period, pushing the combined total of confirmed and suspected measles-related fatalities to 1,378 since the surge began on 15 March 2026. The continuing rise in deaths and new cases has intensified pressure on hospitals and renewed calls for stronger immunisation drives. The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) reported the latest figures for the 24 hours ending at 8:00 a.m. on Friday. All seven of the newest deaths were classified as suspected measles cases; no laboratory-confirmed measles fatalities occurred during that window. Of the overall death toll, 1,272 remain listed as suspected while 106 have been confirmed through laboratory testing. Dhaka and Sylhet divisions each recorded three of the most recent deaths, underscoring the concentration of severe cases in these two regions. Infection numbers remain alarmingly high. During the same 24-hour period, the DGHS logged 1,273 additional people with measles symptoms and 78 new laboratory-confirmed cases. These additions bring the cumulative totals since mid-March to more than 262,800 suspected cases and 26,554 confirmed infections. Hospitals nationwide have admitted 235,482 patients with suspected measles over the course of the outbreak. Of these, 226,440 have recovered and been discharged, showing that timely hospital care saves the large majority of patients. Nevertheless, the steady daily influx continues to stretch paediatric wards and isolation facilities. The current outbreak, which has persisted for nearly nine months, is widely linked to gaps in routine immunisation coverage. ---

items.title: WHO Chief announces Hantavirus outbreak nearing its end
items.excerpt: Saturday, November 28, 2026 WHO Chief announces Hantavirus outbreak nearing its end The World Health Organization (WHO) has announced that the recent Hantavirus outbreak is nearing its conclusion, with no new cases reported among monitored contacts in affected countries. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said that all individuals who had been in contact with the two confirmed cases identified in South Africa have completed their monitoring period without any additional infections being detected. In a statement posted on social media platform X, Ghebreyesus also noted that quarantine and follow-up procedures had been successfully completed in both Spain and Netherlands, including for crew members aboard the vessel MV Hondius. According to the WHO, the total number of confirmed Hantavirus cases remains at 13, including three fatalities. Health officials emphasized that the situation has remained stable in recent weeks, leading to growing confidence that the outbreak is approaching its end. The WHO continues to monitor the situation closely while maintaining surveillance measures to prevent any potential resurgence of infections. Hantavirus is a rare but potentially life-threatening disease transmitted primarily through contact with infected rodents, including mice and rats. The virus can cause severe respiratory and other serious health complications in humans, making rapid detection and containment measures essential during outbreaks. Global health authorities have welcomed the absence of new cases as a positive sign, while urging continued vigilance in areas where exposure to rodent populations remains a public health concern. items.title: The perfect storm behind Congo’s deadliest Ebola outbreak | Health
items.excerpt: Outbreak spiralling out of control The story of Bahati Prince lays bare the merciless unpredictability of Ebola. Since his death this summer in the DRC, the epidemic there has continued to spiral out of control. More than 11,000 infections and 5,300 deaths have been recorded, meaning nearly half of those infected have died. MSF reported on November 12 that nearly two-thirds of reported Ebola-related deaths over the previous month were in communities, not in treatment centres. That means the surveillance network, supposedly the cornerstone of an Ebola response, is blind to the majority of infections. People are dying in their homes surrounded by their families, seeding the next wave of the virus. This is the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak ever to hit Congo and the second worst worldwide. Only the epidemic that swept through West Africa between 2014 and 2016 was more devastating, claiming more than 11,000 lives, according to the World Health Organization. Three different viruses are known to cause large Ebola outbreaks: Ebola virus, also known as Zaire Ebola virus, Sudan virus and Bundibugyo virus. A fourth, Tai Forest virus, can also cause Ebola disease in humans, but only one confirmed human case has been documented. Approved vaccines and virus-specific treatments are available only for Ebola virus; candidates for Sudan and Bundibugyo viruses are still under development. The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which no approved vaccine or treatment exists. Clinical trials have recently begun using Ervebo, a vaccine proven effective against the more common Zaire strain, while researchers work frantically to develop a vaccine specifically for Bundibugyo. Since the outbreak was first detected in May in Ituri province, the virus has spread to eight of the DRC’s 26 provinces.
